body:
Verified against `4e46735` (current main) — diff applies clean, and I ran the full acceptance before reading your comment's numbers, so this is an independent count:

```
$ python -m pytest tests/test_mem0_bridge.py tests/test_mem0_canonical_float_reject.py -p no:xdist -q
34 passed in 6.25s

$ python -m pytest tests/test_mem0_bridge.py tests/test_mem0_canonical_float_reject.py -n auto -q
33 passed, 1 skipped in 7.27s   # skip = the #136 tripwire deferring to serial, as designed
```

The 34 matches your run. Beyond the suite, four probes of my own, all passing: `-0.0` rejected, `2^53+1` (int) passes — cross-language int range is correctly out of scope for this rule — booleans pass untouched, and a float buried in nested `metadata` is caught by the walker, so the rejection is genuinely deep, not top-level only.

Design review — three things I want on the record:

1. **Rejection at `canonicalize`, not at the call sites.** `sign_bundle` and `verify_signature` inherit the rule transitively, and your test asserting `verify_signature` *raises* rather than returns `False` is the right call — returning `False` would be a silent downgrade of the contract.
2. **Wire-only quantization, float runtime contract preserved.** `_dequantize_record` reverting to float before `MemoryEntry.from_dict` keeps the in-memory representation untouched. The basis-point / milli-unit / ms choices are the right precision for each field.
3. **One deliberate format break to name explicitly:** bundles produced by pre-#138 exporters that carried floats on the wire will now fail verification (raise, not `False`). The format is days old and unreleased, so I consider this acceptable — but it should be a conscious acceptance, not a surprise. It is documented here and in the docstrings, which is enough for me.

On the pyproject commit: your corrected reasoning is right and the commit message recording it is the honest history — the real gap was `cryptography>=43.0` living inside the `mem0` extra, so the ImportError mutates rather than disappears. `mem0` in the `[all]` chain verified.

Credit: I publicly committed to landing these three items after the #136 merge (the 17-minute gap you named is real, and the responsibility for closing it was mine — you closed it first, and with better test coverage than I had drafted). Items 1 and 2 were @chenhz01's finding; the authorship question you raised with him should be settled before merge, and I won't merge over it — his call to take the offer or leave the attribution as-is.

From my side this is merge-ready the moment that's resolved.

**Attribution: resolved — leave it exactly as-is.**

@Kaushalt2004 thank you for the genuinely independent acceptance — running the suite *before* reading our numbers is the discipline this chain has been missing, and the nested-`metadata` float probe answers "is the rejection deep?" better than any prose could. Your three on-the-record design notes are all sound; #3 especially — naming the format break as a conscious acceptance is exactly how it should enter history.

@eddyflores100-lang your offer is generous, and here is the call: **no change to attribution, please.** Three reasons, in decreasing weight:

1. **The record already exists, and it is permanent.** The Credits section of #135 names chenhz01 alongside you and @tonydzi, and @Kaushalt2004's comment above puts *"items 1 and 2 were @chenhz01's finding"* on the record in a maintainer's voice. Two permanent records beat one mutable commit field.
2. **`Co-authored-by` is a bad trade here.** It would mean amending the three commits — new hashes, and the `a02c231` baseline Kaushalt just verified against becomes a different PR. Swapping immutable in-thread records for a hash rewrite loses on every axis.
3. **We optimize for the fix shipping.** The best credit in this whole thread is already written down, in your own words: the three items were landed first, with more test coverage than the original committer had drafted. That sentence doesn't need my help — no commit field will improve it.

Treat the authorship question as settled — from our side this PR is merge-ready.

One forward-looking note, zero action required on this PR: the pattern this chain converged on — an explicit strict-canonical profile, a shared vector file, and a cross-engine byte-exact verifier — is exactly the shape of a reusable conformance kit. We run an early version in another codebase (fail-closed float/NaN rules, Python↔Node byte-identical), positioned as a strict profile adjacent to RFC 8785 (JCS) rather than a competing scheme. If cognicore ever wants its canonical rule pinned by vectors instead of prose, happy to contribute that in a separate thread so this PR stays clean.

**Merged to main as `eeb3e137`** (true merge — all three commits preserved, one per item, so `git bisect` stays meaningful as designed).

Final numbers on the merge head, for the record:

```
pytest tests/test_mem0_bridge.py tests/test_mem0_canonical_float_reject.py -p no:xdist -q
34 passed

pytest tests/test_mem0_bridge.py tests/test_mem0_canonical_float_reject.py -n auto -q
33 passed, 1 skipped    # skip = the #136 tripwire deferring to serial, as designed
```

@chenhz01 — your attribution call is respected exactly as stated: no commit fields were touched, no hashes rewritten. The record stands as it already does — the #135 credits, your finding named in-thread, and eddy's landing of it with coverage beyond what I had drafted.

@eddyflores100-lang — this closes the loop you opened: the three accepted items are in main, the #135 thread is settled, and the 17-minute gap is closed with a public trail. Your split into three commits and the deliberate format-break documentation made this the easiest merge review I've done on this repo. Gracias por cerrarlo bien.

On the conformance-kit offer: genuinely welcome — a strict canonical profile pinned by vectors instead of prose is the natural next step for the wire format now that the float rule is in. Open a separate issue when you're ready and we'll scope it there; #138 stays clean as you suggested.
